source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2015) Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity
finding: Partial information framework. Each forecaster reports the expectation of the event given their own information set, so each forecast is calibrated. Differences between forecasts come only from information diversity. The aggregator knows nothing but the forecasts.
numbers: Gaussian partial information model; forecasts p_i = E(1_A | F_i); the loss studied is the Brier score.
limits: Assumes every individual forecast is calibrated and the model is Gaussian. Noise reduction only, bias is set aside.
agent_relevance: Extremizing is a statement about how much information the forecasts hold that is not already shared. It is not a free confidence boost.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2015) Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity
finding: The older measurement-error view treats forecasts as noisy copies of one truth, which leads to plain averaging and an under-confident result. Extremizing was then an ad hoc fix on top. The authors call that model at odds with real forecasting.
numbers: Lists earlier extremizing uses: Ranjan and Gneiting 2010 (beta transform), Satopaa et al 2014 (logit regression), Baron et al 2014, Mellers et al 2014, and older Karmarkar 1978, Erev et al 1994, Shlomi and Wallsten 2010.
limits: Literature framing by the authors, not a new test.
agent_relevance: Samples from one model are close to noisy copies of one information set. That is the case where averaging is right and extremizing is not.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2015) Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity
finding: The oracular aggregator (uses all information of all forecasters) is more likely than not more extreme than the probit average. The extremization ratio is Cauchy distributed and P(ratio>1) is strictly above 1/2. But extremizing is not guaranteed to help on any one question.
numbers: Proposition 4.2: ratio ~ Cauchy(x0, gamma); P(ratio > 1) > 1/2.
limits: Holds under the Gaussian model. A probability above 1/2 is not certainty.
agent_relevance: On a single question extremizing can hurt. Only an average gain over many questions is promised.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2015) Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity
finding: Complete information overlap: all forecasts are identical, so no extremizing is needed. Zero overlap: the optimal aggregate is a weighted vote (range voting) divided by a term that extremizes by total group information. The optimum moves smoothly from averaging to voting as overlap falls.
numbers: Worked example 3.1: optimal aggregate is 2/3 with high overlap and 4/5 with low overlap.
limits: Zero and full overlap are logical extremes, not realistic.
agent_relevance: Same prompt, same model, same context means high overlap, so average and do not extremize.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2015) Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity
finding: With symmetric partial overlap, the amount of extremizing grows with the group's total information and with information diversity. These are two separate drivers. It falls as overlap rises.
numbers: Two-forecaster map of the Cauchy location x0 over total information and overlap. x0 rises with N and with total information, falls with overlap.
limits: Exact only for N=2 with equal information sizes; authors say relaxing this keeps the picture.
agent_relevance: More samples help only if the samples carry different information. Extra identical samples add nothing.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2015) Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity
finding: Real data: 44 super-forecasters, 123 IARPA ACE events (23 happened), 17 to 34 forecasts per event, mean 24.2. Aggregating one event at a time with no training data, the revealed aggregator p_cs had the best Brier score and the plain mean the worst.
numbers: Mean Brier: mean 0.132, logit average 0.128, probit average 0.128, p_cs 0.123. Reliability 0.026, 0.025, 0.023, 0.020. Resolution 0.045, 0.048, 0.047, 0.049. Uncertainty 0.152. Forecasts of 0 and 1 were clipped to 0.001 and 0.999.
limits: One year, one pool of already selected top forecasters, only 23 positive events. No significance test in the text for the 0.009 gap.
agent_relevance: Even in a good pool the gain from a smarter pool is small (about 7% in Brier), so extremizing is a modest lever.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2015) Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity
finding: Authors explain why super-forecaster teams need little or no extremizing: they know a lot and work in groups, so they share information and their forecasts sit near the oracle. Higher self-rated expertise also went with less extremizing needed.
numbers: Qualitative summary of GJP results (Mellers et al 2014; Satopaa et al 2014a,b).
limits: An interpretation, not a direct test inside this paper.
agent_relevance: Strong agreement among good, communicating forecasters means extremizing is least needed. It supports G4: agreement from shared sources is not extra evidence.

source: Satopaa, Ungar (2015) Combining and Extremizing Real-Valued Forecasts
finding: Extends the partial information framework to any real-valued forecast. Weighted averages are marginally consistent but not reliable and do not expand variance, so they sit too close to the marginal mean. Extremizing is redefined as a shift away from the marginal mean, not toward 0 or 1.
numbers: Definition 2.3: X_j extremizes X_i if X_j >= X_i >= mu0 or mu0 >= X_i >= X_j. Theorem 2.2: the weighted average fails reliability and variance expansion.
quote: improves the aggregate if and only if the marginal probability of success is 0.5
limits: Theory under the partial information model; needs the marginal mean as pivot.
agent_relevance: Extremizing has a pivot, the base rate. Pushing away from 0.5 without knowing the base rate can push the wrong way.

source: Satopaa, Ungar (2015) Combining and Extremizing Real-Valued Forecasts
finding: Counter example to the naive rule: if rain falls on 20% of days and the average forecast is 0.30, the aggregate should move toward one, away from the base rate 0.20, not toward zero.
numbers: Base rate 0.20, mean forecast 0.30, correct shift is upward.
limits: Illustration, not data.
agent_relevance: For rare-event questions the agent must push away from the base rate, so it needs a base rate (outside view) before it can extremize at all.

source: Satopaa, Ungar (2015) Combining and Extremizing Real-Valued Forecasts
finding: Extremizing is most likely to help when the single most informed forecaster knows much less than the group knows in total. The method fits weights plus a linear extremizing step (a pivot mu0 and a factor; factor above 1 extremizes) by convex optimization.
numbers: Linear extremizer fitted on training data.
limits: Linear only; authors say a non-linear function could give more gain.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable rule: extremize only if each member is weak and the members differ.

source: Satopaa, Ungar (2015) Combining and Extremizing Real-Valued Forecasts
finding: Real-world test on forecasts from models of a continuous outcome, at no and high information overlap. Averages were unreliable and under-confident. The extremized aggregate recovered reliability. Fitted factor was above 1 in both cases.
numbers: Quadratic loss, no overlap: single models 187.80 and 185.74; mean 155.69; weighted 156.32; extremized 133.23; full-information model 110.91. High overlap: single model 197.03; mean 177.45; weighted 176.59; extremized 169.92. Fitted factor 1.6950 (no overlap) and 1.4382 (high overlap). Reliability term: 31.45 weighted vs 9.86 extremized (no overlap). Uncertainty 278.81.
limits: Real-valued outcome, not event probabilities. One dataset. Gain shrinks with overlap: weighted to extremized is -15% with no overlap and -4% with high overlap.
agent_relevance: Direct numbers: the gain from extremizing was about four times larger with no overlap than with high overlap. Shared inputs mean a small gain.

source: Satopaa, Ungar (2015) Combining and Extremizing Real-Valued Forecasts
finding: Synthetic study: with no information overlap the extremized aggregate used all the group information. With high overlap it did not fully recover it, because it cannot subtract off the shared part.
numbers: No overlap: five forecasters, zero covariance, optimal variance 0.80 equals group information. High overlap (covariance 0.12): group information 0.32, the extremized-weighted average reached only 0.228 variance.
limits: Simulation with a known generating process.
agent_relevance: Shared information caps what any aggregate can recover; extremizing will not recover it.

source: Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne, Jose, Winkler (2018) Bayesian Ensembles of Binary-Event Forecasts: When Is It Appropriate to Extremize or Anti-Extremize?
finding: Bayesian ensembles show that extremizing is not always right. The average double counts the prior (base rate), so extremizing is right when experts use private information only. When experts share information the aggregator lacks, the optimal ensemble can anti-extremize, that is, be less extreme than the average.
numbers: Examples 3 and 6 (normal/normal pair, mu0 = -1.25, expert 1 reports p1 = 0.36): the anti-extremizing region grows as private information becomes shared.
quote: Anti-extremizing emerges (or increases) because of the reduction in the overall sample size
limits: Analytic, shown by examples and figures over conjugate and generalized probit ensembles.
agent_relevance: Direct basis for G4: for correlated samples the right move may be to hold or soften, not extremize.

source: Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne, Jose, Winkler (2018) Bayesian Ensembles of Binary-Event Forecasts: When Is It Appropriate to Extremize or Anti-Extremize?
finding: Two real out-of-sample tests with 10-fold cross validation on three base models (lasso, random forest, xgboost). The best generalized probit ensemble beat the equal-weight average, the optimal linear pool, the beta-transformed pool and the logit aggregator on log score.
numbers: Fannie Mae loans, 1,056,724 records, base rate 8.49%: log score of mean 0.2347, optimal linear pool 0.2330, beta pool 0.2359, logit 0.2329, new ensemble 0.2327, xgboost alone 0.2337. Carvana, 72,983 cars, base rate 12.30%. The ensemble extremized the average in 79.6% (Fannie Mae) and 81.3% (Carvana) of out-of-sample forecasts, so it did the opposite about one time in five.
limits: Base models are statistical models, not people. Gaps are small (0.2347 to 0.2327 is under 1%). No significance tests in the text.
agent_relevance: With members that share all covariates the gain from a clever extremizing step is tiny. The high-overlap case again.

source: Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne, Jose, Winkler (2018) Bayesian Ensembles of Binary-Event Forecasts: When Is It Appropriate to Extremize or Anti-Extremize?
finding: The paper reports that Tetlock and Gardner (2015) found teams that share information well, such as super-forecaster teams, gain little from extremizing, and says its theory matches. It quotes Baron et al. (2014) as the main justification for extremizing: different information behind a common 0.6.
numbers: Quote of Baron et al 2014 p.134, as cited here.
quote: someone who knew all of this would have a right to much higher confidence
limits: Second-hand; the Baron paper itself was closed access this session.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: extremizing is justified only when members used different information.

source: Baron, Mellers, Tetlock, Stone, Ungar (2014) Two Reasons to Make Aggregated Probability Forecasts More Extreme. Decision Analysis 11(2)
finding: Founding paper cited by the others. A publisher summary says one transformation of the aggregate, with different parameters for the mean and the median, can correct two distortions, and that comparing mean and median may help tell them apart. The first distortion is information the forecasters do not share.
numbers: Not read. Only a publisher summary line and citations in opened papers were seen. No numbers recorded.
limits: Closed access; I could not open it. Treat all details as unverified.
agent_relevance: Needs a direct read before we quote numbers from it.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament. Psychological Science
finding: Cited in two opened papers as showing empirically that extremizing improved aggregate forecasts of international events in the IARPA ACE tournament run by the Good Judgment Project.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Second-hand only. Overlaps with the Good Judgment Project subfield (E03/02).
agent_relevance: See subfield 02 for the tournament; here only the extremizing step matters.

source: Ranjan, Gneiting (2010) Combining probability forecasts. J. Royal Statistical Society B 72
finding: Cited as showing the linear opinion pool is under-confident (not extreme enough) and proposing a beta-transformed linear pool to fix it. Hora (2004) is cited for the same point.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Second-hand only, through the Lichtendahl et al. and Satopaa et al. texts.
agent_relevance: An average of calibrated inputs is itself not calibrated, so an extra monotone map is needed. The same applies to an agent that averages its own samples.

source: Neyman, Roughgarden (2023) From Proper Scoring Rules to Max-Min Optimal Forecast Aggregation
finding: Each proper scoring rule has a matching pool (quasi-arithmetic pooling). The quadratic score goes with linear pooling and the log score goes with logarithmic (geometric) pooling. The pool should follow the scoring rule the user cares about.
numbers: Weather example: an informed model says 0.1%, a less informed model says 20%. Equal-weight linear pool gives about 10%; log pool gives about 1.6%. Score difference at report 0.7: quadratic 0.8, log (scaled) 0.61.
limits: Theory with a worst-case guarantee; no empirical data. It does not test extremizing as such.
agent_relevance: If extremes matter, pool in log space; this pulls the pool toward the confident low-probability member.

source: Neyman, Roughgarden (2023) From Proper Scoring Rules to Max-Min Optimal Forecast Aggregation
finding: The score of a quasi-arithmetic pool is concave in the weights, so weights can be learned online by gradient descent with low regret. The class of such pools is characterised by axioms that generalise Kolmogorov's quasi-arithmetic means.
numbers: Concavity result and regret bound (see paper).
limits: Needs repeated scored outcomes.
agent_relevance: An agent with a scored history could learn member weights. A single run has no such history.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Study 1: the median of 12 LLMs on 31 binary questions, compared with 925 human forecasters from a three-month tournament. The LLM crowd beat the 50% no-information benchmark and was statistically equal to the human crowd.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs 0.25 for always 50%: t(30) = -2.35, p = 0.026. Human crowd median Brier 0.19 (SD 0.19): t(60) = 0.19, p = 0.850. ANOVA over models and humans F(12,354) = 2.64, p = 0.002; Coral (Command) was worst.
limits: Only 31 questions. Equivalence is shown with medium-effect bounds (d = 0.5), which is loose. Models differ in training date and search access.
agent_relevance: Aggregating different models (more diverse information) works. That is the sound analogue of the human crowd, unlike resampling one model.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: LLMs showed acquiescence bias: mean predictions well above 50% though about half of questions resolved yes. The aggregate was over-confident and most models were poorly calibrated. The median still beat the baseline.
numbers: Calibration index per model (lower is better): Falcon-180B 0.027, Qwen-7B-Chat 0.055, PaLM 2 Chat 0.068, Llama-2-70B 0.071, GPT-4 0.075.
limits: Shared bias is not removed by taking the median. This is correlated error across models.
agent_relevance: Pushing a biased-high aggregate away from 0.5 would make it worse. This data does not support extremizing an LLM crowd (G4).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Study 2: giving GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median as information improved their accuracy by 17% to 28%, but simply averaging the human and machine forecasts was more accurate than the models' own updating.
numbers: Improvement 17% to 28% in accuracy; averaging beat model updating (per-model values in the paper).
limits: The human median was taken within 48 hours of the community prediction; small question set.
agent_relevance: Average the agent's own estimate with an outside estimate instead of letting the outside number replace its reasoning.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Retrieval plus reasoning plus fine-tuned model. The final forecast is a trimmed mean of 6 forecasts. Five ensemble rules were compared on a validation set.
numbers: Brier: mean 0.1656, median 0.1651, geometric mean 0.1655, trimmed mean 0.1649, USC (a model merges the answers) 0.1691, no ensemble 0.1676, human crowd 0.1600. Spread among the four numeric rules is 0.0007.
limits: Validation set only; differences are inside noise. Their trimmed mean is non-standard (furthest forecast gets half weight). Only 6 inputs.
agent_relevance: The choice of numeric rule matters little. An LM-based merge (USC) was worse than no ensemble.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: The system is naturally well calibrated. Standard calibration fixes (binning, isotonic regression) did not improve it. Averaging with the crowd helped: weighted average with 4x crowd weight moved the test Brier from 0.149 (crowd alone) to 0.146.
numbers: Test Brier: system 0.179, crowd 0.149, combination 0.146. Five or more articles: system 0.238 vs crowd 0.240. Under all three conditions (crowd uncertain, early retrieval, 5+ articles; 22% of forecasts): system 0.240, crowd 0.247, unweighted combination 0.237.
limits: Subsets chosen after the fact; weights tuned on validation. Table column layout in the PDF text is partly ambiguous.
agent_relevance: When forecasts are already calibrated, recalibration or extremizing adds nothing. Averaging with a distinct source helps more.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities (ICLR 2025)
finding: LLM ensemble baseline of 9 forecasts (3 models x 3 prompts). Median, trimmed mean, geometric mean and geometric mean of log odds (the Satopaa 2014 rule) were compared. The two geometric rules scored best, by a small margin.
numbers: Brier on the Halawi test set: median 0.197, trimmed mean 0.197, geometric mean 0.194, geometric mean of log odds 0.194 (2 SE about 0.024). Single models: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 0.178, GPT-4o 0.207, Gemini-1.5-Pro 0.214. The ensemble was worse than the best single model.
limits: Differences of 0.003 are far below 2 SE. The ensemble includes weaker models. No extremizing step was tested.
agent_relevance: Pooling with a weaker member can lose to the best member. Log-odds pooling is the usual first step before any extremizing.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities (ICLR 2025)
finding: Humans vs LLMs on 200 questions at 4 horizons: the super-forecaster median beat the public median and the best LLM.
numbers: Brier: super-forecasters 0.096, public 0.121 (p<0.001), best LLM Claude-3.5-Sonnet with freeze values 0.122. Best LLM without the crowd forecast 0.136.
limits: Top LLMs had access to the market crowd forecast on market questions.
agent_relevance: The bar for an LLM aggregate is a super-forecaster median, which already needs little extremizing.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: N=991 people answered 6 forecast questions with an LLM assistant (a super-forecasting prompt or a noisy, base-rate-neglecting one) or a control. Both assistants raised individual accuracy. The authors tested whether this herds forecasters and hurts crowd aggregation. The data did not consistently support that.
numbers: Accuracy up 24% to 28% vs control; 41% (superforecasting) vs 29% (noisy) without outlier Question 3. Mean of medians: superforecasting 0.52, noisy 0.41, control 0.55 (outlier included).
quote: this aggregation tends to be most effective when there is a diversity of independent forecasts
limits: One shared LLM could correlate human errors. The authors raised it as a risk and found no consistent evidence. Six questions; one outlier item dominated.
agent_relevance: The same worry as G4 in human form: a shared source correlates forecasts and cuts the value of aggregation.

source: Paleka, Sudhir, Alvarez, Bhat, Shen, Tramer (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Consistency checks (logical relations between questions) give a score that needs no outcomes. Average consistency violation tracks Brier score across forecasters.
numbers: Aggregated arbitrage and frequentist scores plotted against Brier (Fig 3). Exact values not recorded.
limits: Only part of the paper was read. No extremizing test.
agent_relevance: A cheap check an agent could run on its own set of forecasts before pooling them.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (ICLR 2023)
finding: Majority vote over sampled reasoning paths from one model beats greedy decoding on reasoning tasks. This is voting, not probability pooling.
numbers: GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2%, StrategyQA +6.4%, ARC-challenge +3.9%.
limits: Single-answer tasks scored by answer match. No calibration or extremizing was measured. Samples from one model are correlated.
agent_relevance: Voting over samples raises accuracy, but the vote share is not a probability. Do not extremize it (G4).
